note: Scoring-to-picture rules: general film-scoring practice, not drawn from the four books. Each rule is marked own.

rules.text: Let tension follow the amount of movement: more layers, a higher register and louder dynamics as the picture gets busier; thin out when it stills.
Play against the picture sparingly: slow, sustained music under frantic movement reads as irony or dread. Use it only when the mood reading supports that.
Place the climax on the clip's strongest peak reading, not merely on its busiest stretch, and build toward it across the section before.
Give a short clip one climax. Lesser peaks get an accent or a lift in register, not a second climax.
Treat a scene cut that brings lasting change as a section boundary: change harmony, texture or theme there. A cut inside continuous action needs at most an accent.
Land accents exactly on the picture's hit points; an accent slightly early or late looks like a mistake. Do not mark every movement: too many hits turn comic.
For playful or absurd pictures, tight synchronisation is welcome: staccato, pizzicato and sudden stops that copy the movement read as humour.
Under a frozen pose or a held shot, hold or thin the music: a sustained chord or a pedal lets the picture breathe.
Take the tempo from repeating movement when the picture has a steady pulse. Bodies often move at half or double the beat, so prefer the candidate nearest a natural tempo for the mood.
When the picture has no convincing pulse, choose the tempo from mood and energy, and let phrase boundaries, not beats, carry the synchronisation.
To land on a cut, prefer the least audible fix: a tempo change under two percent goes unnoticed; beyond that, lengthen or shorten a phrase by a bar.
Holding a chord into a cut builds expectation. Use it when the picture also pauses, or when the next section should arrive with force.
A pickup bar suits a cut into higher energy: the extra bar leans into the new section.
When the picture has a steady pulse, keep the tempo fixed and adjust phrase lengths instead, so the beats stay with the movement.
Match register to body level: low, grounded movement suits low registers; reaching, rising or airborne movement suits high ones.
Match articulation to movement quality: flowing wants legato lines, sharp wants staccato and accents, shaking wants tremolo, bouncing wants a clear pulse.
Give a recurring move its own recurring musical idea, and bring that idea back, varied, each time the move returns.
During playback make only small refinements: one accent on an unmarked hit, a slight lift or drop. Never fight the composed phrase.
End with the picture: if it stops abruptly, stop; if it holds or fades, let the last chord ring past the final frame.
Judge movement from the differences between consecutive images, not from how dramatic a single pose looks. A striking still pose is not movement.
A cut changes the whole frame at once and stays changed: new background, new framing. Fast movement changes only where the subject is.
